title: What is known about 1RB0LA_0RC1LF_0RD0LA_1LD0LE_1RB1LF_---1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LA_0RC1LF_0RD0LA_1LD0LE_1RB1LF_---1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves two of the shift rules the run uses and the situations that lead to a halt (kernel), and no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in 109 steps.

What it does. The tape is a list of short blocks of 1s (lengths 2 to 7) separated by single 0s, with a few runs of the words 0111 and 1110. The head does not sweep the whole tape in one go: it travels in zig-zags, for example leftwards 8 cells every 44 steps, rewriting the blocks it passes, and the right end advances 8 cells at a time. The list of block lengths has no visible order.
Where a halt would come from. Only F reading a 0 halts. F is entered from B or E reading a 1, so 0 B>1 and 0 E>1 halt at once. In 2·108 steps F always reads a 1.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: D with 0 two left, 1 left, 1 under the head. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 31,638 cells have been visited and 24,079 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.423). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.515).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: C with a 0 behind it walks right through any block of 1s, three steps a cell, carrying the 0 along; C turns each 0111 into 1110, ten steps a copy.

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: 0 B>1 and 0 E>1 halt after one step, 0 1 1 D>0 after three.

claims.title: F never reads a 0 in 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: In the first 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps the machine is in state F 9,297,309 times, every time on a 1: the halting transition F0 is never close to firing in a way the run shows.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. No macro structure is known: the tape content looks random and the decider pipeline (including NGramCPS with n ≤ 10 here) leaves it open.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine works its way back and forth over a tape of short blocks of 1s, and the blocks look random. This page runs it in your browser and shows the two moves it uses most.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 31,638 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Moves over blocks of 1s
html: The tape is mostly short blocks of 1s, 2 to 7 long, each followed by a single 0. State C, with a 0 just behind it, walks right through a block and carries the 0 along, three steps a cell:
(Lean: walk_ones, for blocks of any length.) In runs of the word 0111, C turns each copy into 1110, ten steps a copy (shift_0111).
These moves keep the blocks, but the head does not just sweep: it zig-zags locally, and the list of block lengths changes in a way nobody has described.

sections.heading: F must read a 0
html: Only F reading a 0 halts. F is entered by B or E reading a 1 and moving left, so the machine halts as soon as B or E reads a 1 with a 0 to its left:
In the run F is entered 9.3 million times in the first 2·108 steps, always on a 1.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.423). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.515).
After 109 steps the tape spans 31,638 cells (5,963 left of the start, 17,415 right), with a density of 1s of 0.761.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Two-sided bouncer over short blocks of 1s (lengths 2 to 7) separated by single 0s, with runs of 0111/1110; the head works in local zig-zags and the content looks random. Open.
